To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HINT can be used to predict the affinities among ERs and different ERE sequences and to analyze the role played by different atoms in these interactions.
HINT can be used to analyze the binding of ERα and/or ERβ with different sequences, and that the results obtained are in agreement with experimental data.
HINT is a useful tool to analyze the interactions between ERs and different ERE sequences and to identify the most important residues for the binding event.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the application of Hints force field for the simulation of protein‐DNA complexes and with the development of a new strategy to analyze their interactions.

the application of computational chemistry to the simulation and analysis, in terms of binding affinity, of the complexes formed by the DNA‐binding domains of estrogen receptors (ERα and ERβ) and different estrogen responsive element (ERE) sequences.
the application of HADDOCK, a docking program, and HINT, a force field, to the simulation and analysis, respectively, of the interaction between ERα and ER β with ERE sequences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HINT force field, in combination with the homology modeling approach, is a useful and powerful tool for the prediction of ER‐ERE interactions.
HINT is a useful and powerful tool for the prediction of binding affinities, as well as for the analysis of the role played by the different amino acid and nucleotide atoms in the interaction.
HINT is a very useful tool for the simulation and the analysis of protein‐DNA interactions, in particular for the study of ERE‐ER complexes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the computational methods are able to predict the affinities for different EREs and to identify the positions in the ERE sequences that are most important to ER binding.

HINT is a powerful tool that can be used to analyze and quantify the contribution of each single atom of the protein and the nucleotides in a DNA binding event.
